profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a digital wealth management firm about launching a six-week internal pilot of a new allocation engine for high-volatility assets. The engine is based on maximizing typical long-run capital growth under multiplicative Brownian motion, and the team now needs to decide how the pilot will be structured, which asset universe it will cover, how allocations will be expressed in the advisor workflow, what rebalancing operations will look like, and what materials will be prepared for compliance and advisor enablement. The agenda is to align on pilot scope, portfolio construction boundaries, implementation timeline, and ownership of deliverables. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan for the pilot launch package, rebalance process, and handoff dates for research, product, and compliance preparation.

members.name: Dana Liu
members.expertise: Advisor workflow design, portfolio product launches, compliance coordination, retail investment UX
members.background: Dana has spent eight years shipping managed-investing features at brokerages and robo-advisors, and now oversees how quantitative strategies are packaged into advisor-facing tools.
members.private_state: Dana wants a smooth pilot that advisors can explain simply and compliance can approve quickly, while avoiding any operational surprises that would delay the quarter's launch calendar.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'risky assets,' they mean the narrow sleeve already discussed in product roadmaps: crypto ETFs and leveraged commodity ETPs, not the whole high-volatility tradable universe.
The 'fraction in risky assets' should be shown as a share of the investable sleeve after client cash buffers and mandated reserves are set aside, because that is how advisors talk about allocations.
A 'monthly rebalance' in operations means generating orders on the first business day of the month using the prior month-end snapshot, not trading at the month-end close itself.
If the allocation outputs are directionally sensible and simple enough to explain, the weights are 'stable' for pilot purposes even if exact percentages are occasionally adjusted behind the scenes.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Stochastic portfolio theory, growth-optimal allocation, volatility modeling, backtesting for multi-asset strategies
members.background: Arjun previously led quantitative allocation research at a hedge fund and joined the firm to translate academic portfolio models into systematic investment products.
members.private_state: Arjun wants the pilot to preserve the theoretical integrity of the growth-rate framework and worries that product simplifications will distort the strategy enough to make the pilot results meaningless.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'risky assets,' they mean the model's full eligible set of instruments above the volatility threshold, including volatile single-name equities, crypto ETFs, and leveraged exchange-traded products.
The 'fraction in risky assets' is mathematically defined as a portion of total account capital, because the optimal leverage and cash share are only meaningful relative to the entire portfolio base.
A 'monthly rebalance' means a month-end batch aligned with the backtest convention, using end-of-month prices and updating weights at that boundary.

If the ranking and sign of asset weights remain consistent and the long-run growth objective holds under rolling estimation windows, the portfolio is 'stable' enough, even if displayed percentages move substantially month to month.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the risky-asset universe
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the risky assets' as if the category is already obvious.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the pilot will only cover the new high-risk product sleeve already slated for launch: crypto ETFs and leveraged commodity ETPs available in advisor-managed brokerage accounts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the model will optimize across the broader high-volatility universe already used in research, including crypto ETFs, leveraged ETPs, and volatile single-name equities such as biotech and AI names above the volatility cutoff.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both believe prior strategy discussions already fixed the universe, and 'risky assets' sounds like a settled business label rather than a boundary that needs restating.

misalignment_points.topic: What the risky fraction is a fraction of
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both use the phrase 'fraction of capital in risky assets' and cite example percentages like 35% or 40%.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 interprets 40% as 40% of the investable sleeve after cash reserves, sweep balances, and client-imposed minimum liquidity buffers have been excluded from the denominator.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 interprets 40% as 40% of the account's total capital, with cash and risky assets jointly determined from the same full-capital base.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The percentage itself sounds concrete, and both are accustomed to their own denominator convention being standard, so neither thinks to specify what the base capital includes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the pilot should use a 'monthly rebalance' to keep it simple.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes operations will calculate model weights from month-end data but generate and route trades on the first business day of the next month during normal order windows.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the production process will mirror the research convention and rebalance at the month-end close using end-of-month prices as the execution boundary.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see 'monthly' as the important planning-level choice, while the exact execution timestamp feels like routine implementation detail handled elsewhere.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a stable allocation for the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the model outputs need to be 'stable enough for advisors' before the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks stability means the visible allocation mix should not swing enough to create confusing month-to-month advisor conversations, roughly keeping asset weights within a narrow presentation band.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks stability means the optimizer preserves the same broad asset preference ordering and long-run growth logic across rolling windows, even if the actual percentages change materially.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same reassuring business phrase 'stable enough,' and each assumes the other shares the obvious practical meaning from their own function.
